chain.label: Strong gusty southerly winds at BDL forcing use of runway 15
chain.trigger: winds 170 degrees at 25 knots gusts to 40 knots... The runway 15 approach to BDL is used primarily when the winds are such that the speed and direction preclude the safe use of the airport's primary runway (06/24).

chain.label: Runway 15 VOR final approach course crosses Peak Mountain ridge with 60-ft trees, 2.54 nm from threshold
chain.trigger: The controlling obstacle in the final segment ... was 739 feet of terrain and an additional 80 feet tree height, for a total height of 819 feet msl. This is the ridge line and trees that the flight 1572 initially struck.

caused_by.evidence: The BDL runway 15 VOR approach is used most often when the speed and direction of the winds preclude the use of the primary runway 06/24.

chain.label: FAA approach design deficiencies: no VDP published, no precipitous-terrain adjustment, ridge not depicted on chart
chain.trigger: An examination of FAA records revealed no reason for the absence of a VDP for the approach to runway 15 at BDL... The FAA did not adjust the BDL VOR runway 15 approach MDA for precipitous terrain.

chain.label: Instrument conditions with low overcast and moderate rain on final
chain.trigger: cloud bases were near 2,000 feet with multiple cloud layers above... Flight visibility was near 0 miles in the clouds and 2 to 3 statute miles below the lowest cloud base. Moderate rain probably occurred along the approach

chain.label: Approach flown at 0055 in darkness with no visual terrain cues
chain.trigger: The initial tree strike occurred at approximately 41 degrees, 58.22 minutes north latitude and 072 degrees, 44.38 minutes west longitude during the hours of darkness.

chain.label: Atmospheric pressure falling rapidly at BDL, making issued altimeter settings stale
chain.trigger: pressure falling rapidly... The atmospheric pressure continued to drop and was calculated to be 29.24 inches Hg. at the time of the accident.

chain.label: Approach controller failed to issue the current altimeter setting on initial contact or any update
chain.trigger: The TRACON approach controller did not issue a current altimeter setting to flight 1572 upon initial radio contact with the flight at 0043:49. At that time, the DASI readout indicated a setting of 29.38 inches Hg.

caused_by.evidence: considering the fact that the pressure changes were described by the weather observer as 'pressure falling rapidly'... it would have been prudent for the approach controller to have issued the altimeter setting changes as the airplane neared the airport.

chain.label: Flightcrew never requested a current altimeter setting despite knowing pressure was falling rapidly
chain.trigger: the Safety Board concludes that the flightcrew's failure to request a current altimeter setting from the approach controller was a contributing factor in this accident.

caused_by.evidence: because they knew that the atmospheric pressure was falling rapidly, the flightcrew should have requested a current altimeter setting
the flightcrew should have requested a current altimeter setting from the BDL approach controller when one was not given by the controller, as required, upon initial radio contact

chain.label: Primary altimeters set to a 54-minute-old QFE value read about 76 ft high
chain.trigger: the indicated altitude (height above airport elevation) that the airplane's QFE altimeter was indicating was about 76 feet too high (based on the altimeter setting received at 0030), resulting in the airplane being 76 feet lower than indicated on the primary altimeters.

caused_by.evidence: The atmospheric pressure continued to drop and was calculated to be 29.24 inches Hg. at the time of the accident.
If the controller had issued the current altimeter setting on initial contact, the aircraft would most likely have been 40 feet higher than it actually was when it struck the trees.
these altimeter settings were 29 minutes old when the flightcrew received them and 54 minutes old when the airplane struck the trees on the ridge line.

chain.label: Captain held a constant 1,100 fpm autopilot vertical-speed descent toward MDA with no VDP computed
chain.trigger: a descent rate of about 1,100 feet per minute was initiated by the flightcrew from about 1,840 feet msl and was maintained until tree contact... in this case, no VDP was calculated

caused_by.evidence: if the flightcrew had computed a visual descent point (VDP) for their approach to runway 15... the DME associated with a VDP would have provided the flightcrew with a specific point in space to leave the MDA for landing.

chain.label: First officer left the instruments to search for the runway before MDA and omitted the 100-above-MDA callout
chain.trigger: the first officer did not follow additional company procedures by also calling out 100 feet above MDA... the first officer began looking for the airport prior to reaching the MDA in the critical stages of the descent to MDA, and he was not adequately monitoring the flight instruments to serve as an additional backup to the captain.

caused_by.evidence: There would be no reason for the first officer or the captain to be looking away from the instruments and out the windscreen for the airport until just before or at the VDP.
as the airplane was 'at the base of the clouds,' he began looking for the field visually
The initial tree strike occurred ... during the hours of darkness.

chain.label: Airplane descended about 309 ft below the 908-ft MDA without the required visual references
chain.trigger: they allowed the airplane to descend about 309 feet below the indicated MDA for the instrument approach... the flightcrew's failure to maintain the required MDA until the required visual references identified with the runway were in sight directly caused this accident.

caused_by.evidence: resulting in the airplane being 76 feet lower than indicated on the primary altimeters
Information from the DFDR indicates that a constant rate of descent of 1,100 feet per minute was maintained until the first officer uttered his 'you're going below your….' statement.

if the first officer had monitored the approach on instruments until reaching MDA... he would have been better able to notice and immediately call the captain's attention to the altitude deviation below the MDA.

chain.label: Captain did not recognize the descent below MDA and reacted too late to arrest it
chain.trigger: The captain initially did not recognize the descent below MDA, and he failed to react immediately when he was alerted to the altitude deviation by the first officer. The captain never took manual control of the airplane to either arrest his descent at the MDA or to initiate a more positive and immediate recovery

caused_by.evidence: When he looked back at the instrument panel, he saw that the airplane had descended below MDA.
he was not adequately monitoring the flight instruments to serve as an additional backup to the captain

chain.label: Airplane struck treetops on the ridge 2.54 nm northwest of runway 15
chain.trigger: The initial impact mark from the airplane was with a tree located on the top of Peak Mountain Ridge, approximately 2.54 nautical miles northwest of the approach end of runway 15.

caused_by.evidence: the trees in the area of initial impact were approximately 60 feet tall... the tree was determined to have broken at 770.5 feet [msl]
At that time the airplane was about 350 feet above the ground and 5 seconds away from contact with the trees.
that feature of the autopilot was not engaged until after the first officer uttered his 'you're going below your....' statement

chain.label: Both engines lost power after the tree strike; airplane landed short on the stopway, destroying the ILS antenna array
chain.trigger: power from one engine failed almost immediately after the tree strike, and power from the other engine failed shortly thereafter... The airplane clipped the top of a tree near the end of the runway, impacted and destroyed most of the ILS antenna array... and landed on the edge of the stopway.

caused_by.evidence: the left engine rolled back to a low power level shortly after the ridge line tree impact due to low pressure compressor damage

chain.label: One passenger minor injury; airplane substantially damaged (about $9 million)
chain.trigger: Minor 0 0 1 0 1... damage to the airplane amounted to approximately $9,000,000.

caused_by.evidence: the excellent crew resource management and flight skills that the flightcrew used... were directly responsible for limiting the number of injured passengers to one individual.
